Methyldopa has the advantage of reassuring long-term safety results in the infant, whereas there have been con- cerns about fetal growth retardation with beta blockers, particularly with atenolol.85-87 Nifedipine81,88 or hydralazine81 may also be used. Diuretics are not generally recommended for controlling hypertension in pregnancy because of the theoretical risk of exacerbating the volume depletion of pre-eclampsia; however, they appear to be safe in practice and may be used if necessary.1,83 For patients with pre-eclampsia81,89-92 the definitive treat- ment is delivery (although pre-eclampsia may also devel- op post-partum92), but where the maternal condition al- lows this is usually delayed to allow fetal maturation. Antihypertensive therapy is therefore given to reduce the risk of maternal complications, and prophylactic anticon- vulsants, particularly magnesium sulfate, may also be giv- en in those at high risk for eclampsia (see p.470). Evidence to guide choice of antihypertensive in severe hypertension is limited.93 Oral therapy may be appropriate, in which case methyldopa or beta blockers (preferably labetalol5,92) are usually first-line; calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine are an alternative. However, in acute pre-ec- lampsia or if delivery is imminent, parenteral antihyper- tensives are required. Intravenous hydralazine is widely used,2,92 although there is some evidence that it may be less effective and have more adverse effects than other drugs,94 and some guidelines recommend that it should be avoided.5 Intravenous labetalol and oral nifedipine are also used, and sodium nitroprusside may be required in some patients.2,5 Glyceryl trinitrate may be used if there is pul- monary oedema.5 Other drugs that have been given in- clude diazoxide and clonidine. Prevention of pre-eclampsia. It was hoped that prevention of pre-eclampsia might be possible by reducing the local platelet aggregation thought to be responsible for some of its manifestations. Several small studies suggested that low-dose aspirin reduced the risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension and intra-uterine growth retardation in high- risk patients.95 However, larger studies in women at lower risk generally failed to confirm this benefit96,97 and in one97 the risk of placental abruption was higher in those taking aspirin.
